title: Let Us Resolve Conflicts with Mutual Understanding and Peace

sections.title: A New Vision for Understanding Conflict
content: The speaker explained that knowing which needs of the participating persons were not met is more important than the question of who won and who lost in the conflict. Behind mutually opposing opinions there may also be ordinary human needs such as respect, safety, and recognition. Listening to those needs is the first step for resolution.

sections.title: Listening Patiently in Mediation
content: The speaker explained about meetings with authorities on a problem, further consultations, and efforts made to allocate time. This context suggests that even if a final decision does not come immediately, continuing the conversation is necessary to make the experiences of the affected persons heard and to take them to the attention of the decision-makers. Since the details are unclear as part of the captions, a specific result is not announced here.

sections.title: Separating Opinion from Fact
content: Immediately after hearing the other person’s word a judgment forms in the mind. But the three matters of what really happened, what meaning we gave to it, and what feeling arose in us should be seen separately. When this difference is known, aggression in the conversation decreases and clarity in explaining the problem increases.

sections.title: Giving Space to the Words of Two Groups
content: In the story of two groups differing with each other, the speaker mentioned the manner in which the mediator patiently listened to each one’s word and spoke again with the other group. Listening does not mean accepting every accusation as true. Recognizing the important needs of each group and beginning conversation on possible requests. Through this the fixed enemy images may gradually loosen.

sections.title: Spirituality and Social Responsibility
content: The speaker connected the spiritual vision that there is opportunity for change in every person with social conversation. It was suggested that others should be seen as persons who can take responsibility and grow, without defining them merely with past actions. This is not a command that the harm that occurred should be forgiven; it is exploring a path that does not lead to further violence while clearly recognizing the harm.

sections.title: The Person and the System He Represents
content: Pavan Kumar explained that when meeting an authority, his personal response should not be equated with the whole system’s decision. A person may listen to our word carefully and yet be unable to approve our request because of organizational limitations. Then concluding “he is against us” becomes simplifying the reality.

In conversation we should observe with whom we are speaking, what authorities they have, and which decisions are not in their hands. Knowing the obstacles in the system clearly rather than labeling a person’s personality is useful for the subsequent action. This distinction is specially important in social movements, office disputes, and government-related meetings.

sections.title: The Funds Example of Speaking with a Clear Need
content: The speaker explained a story in which help was obtained by clearly stating the need in a short time in a meeting held for funds. What he mainly showed in this example is not the number of words, but clarity of intention. When matters such as for which work help is needed, what its effect is, and why the other person’s time is valuable are clear, the conversation can proceed forward.

Details such as the financial amount mentioned in the story and the sequence of events should be confirmed with the original video before publication. Even so the teaching is clear: one should speak without hiding the need in our request and without filling the time with accusations. At the same time it should also be remembered the commentary made by the speaker that not every method used in the conversation should be taken as an ideal merely because a result came.

sections.title: Three Hours of Inward Practice to Change the Enemy Image
content: The speaker mentioned the example in which Marshall Rosenberg examined the judgments within himself for about three hours before meeting a person who caused him intense intolerance. This story reminds us that anger and a feeling of enmity can come even to a person who teaches NVC. What is important is not that such a feeling never comes; it is working within oneself when it comes without immediately dealing under its influence.

The story proceeded that in a dispute related to an educational institution Rosenberg became ready to understand their fears and needs, rather than with the intention of defeating the opposite side. Even if the first conversation did not happen easily he again recalled his goal. This example provides a strong context for the message “see the person, listen to the need.”

sections.title: Observing Behavior, Not Judging the Person
content: If a work did not happen, “the work did not happen” is observation; “he is a useless person” is a judgment on the person. The speaker discussed the difference between these two in detail. After turning a person into a label, the interest to know his situation, needs, and obstacles decreases. Only when the behavior that happened is stated clearly is there opportunity to speak for the resolution of the problem.

In this context the speaker mentioned a comparison with the teachings of Jiddu Krishnamurti. However, without confirming the words appearing in the captions as his direct quotation, we are keeping only the essence of the meaning here. The point mainly stands that observation should be useful for clearly understanding the situation, not for deciding a person’s value.
